title: Gold vs Commodities: 100 Years of Prices in Gold Terms
notes: This video uses a SINGLE continuous animated line chart ('horse race') as the primary visual throughout. The chart shows 9 asset/gold ratios racing forward through time (1925-2025). Scenes below define overlays, zoom levels, timeline speed, and event markers ON TOP of the continuous chart. The chart itself is a custom Remotion component (HorseRaceChart) that receives the full ratio dataset and renders all 9 lines simultaneously. Scene transitions are NOT cuts between different visuals — they are zoom/speed changes within the same chart.

scenes.voiceover: The Dow Jones has gained twenty-six thousand percent since 1925. Sounds like the greatest investment in history, right? But what if I told you — when you price the Dow in gold — it has only doubled. That's it. One hundred years. One hundred and thirty-two percent. Less than one percent a year.

visual.description: Full-screen dramatic text reveal. Giant '26,000%' in green, then it deflates/morphs into '132%' with gold shimmer. Dark background.

scenes.notes: NO chart yet. Pure text impact. The 26,000% number should feel massive, then the deflation to 132% is the gut punch. Gold particle effect on the transition.

scenes.voiceover: Here's the idea: forget dollars. Dollars lose value every single year. Instead, let's price everything — stocks, oil, silver, platinum — in gold. How many ounces of gold does it take to buy one unit of each asset? This strips away all the inflation noise and shows you what actually gained real value — and what didn't. I crunched a hundred years of daily data — over a hundred and seventy-five thousand data points — and the results will change how you think about wealth. Let's race them.

visual.description: Animated formula card: 'Asset Price ÷ Gold Price = Gold Ratio' with example (Oil $67 ÷ Gold $2990 = 0.022 oz). Then transition to the horse race starting gate — all 9 asset lines appear at their starting positions (1925), labeled, color-coded. Camera zooms in close. Lines are at the gate, ready to race.
visual.textOverlay: Asset Price ÷ Gold Price = Gold Ratio

scenes.notes: The formula should animate in piece by piece. Then the chart fades in behind — first the grid, then the time axis, then the asset lines pop in one by one with their labels. End with the 'starting gate' view — zoomed in on 1925, all lines ready. This is where the chart component first appears.

scenes.voiceover: For the first half of this story, gold's price was fixed by the government. Twenty dollars and sixty-seven cents an ounce. So every ratio here is a pure reflection of supply and demand — no inflation tricks. In 1925, the Dow-to-Gold ratio starts at six. Stocks are climbing. But then — the Great Depression. The ratio crashes. In 1934, Roosevelt devalues the dollar — gold jumps to thirty-five dollars overnight — and the ratio drops to three. After World War Two, Bretton Woods pegs the entire global economy to gold. Slowly, stocks recover. By the late sixties, the Dow is pushing past twenty times gold. The Nikkei is at fifty-eight times gold — Japan's post-war miracle is real, and it's leading the race by a mile. But behind the scenes, America is printing money to fund Vietnam. The gold standard is cracking.

scenes.voiceover: On August fifteenth, nineteen seventy-one, Nixon goes on television and severs the dollar from gold. The gold standard is dead. Gold is free. And it explodes. From thirty-five dollars to over eight hundred in less than a decade. Watch the race now. Every single line — every asset — plummets. The Dow-to-Gold ratio goes from twenty down to one. The S&P from two point three to zero point one two. The DAX drops ninety-five percent. Even platinum — which was worth nearly seven times gold — falls below gold for the first time ever. And then comes January twenty-second, nineteen eighty. The single most dramatic day in a hundred years of data. On that day, one ounce of gold could buy the entire Dow Jones Industrial Average. One to one. Every asset ratio bottomed out — simultaneously. Gold crushed everything at once.

scenes.voiceover: Then the pendulum swings the other way. Hard. Volcker hikes interest rates to twenty percent. Inflation dies. Stocks take off. And gold just sits there — doing nothing — for twenty years. The Dow-to-Gold ratio explodes from one to forty-five. It's the greatest stock bull run in history. The DAX goes from zero point five to twenty-eight. The Nikkei — remember, it was already leading the race — hits ninety-seven times gold in December nineteen eighty-nine. Ninety-seven. That's the Japanese asset bubble at its peak, and it's the highest any ratio ever reached in this entire dataset. Then Japan crashes. The Nikkei-to-Gold ratio falls from ninety-seven to twelve. A loss of eighty-seven percent — even in gold terms. Japan's miracle turns into Japan's lost decades. Meanwhile, on August twenty-fifth, nineteen ninety-nine — the Dow-to-Gold ratio peaks at forty-four point eight eight. Gold's single worst day in a century. Nobody wants it. Stocks are king.

scenes.voiceover: The dot-com crash. Nine-eleven. The two-thousand-eight financial crisis. COVID. Through crisis after crisis, gold climbs back while everything else struggles. The Dow-to-Gold ratio falls from forty-five back to about fourteen. Commodities get destroyed. Platinum — which started at nearly seven times gold in nineteen sixty-eight — hits an all-time low of zero point three three. Just three weeks ago. A ninety-five percent collapse. Oil touches near zero in gold terms when prices go negative in April twenty-twenty. Silver hits its lowest point versus gold during COVID — worse than the Great Depression. Not a single commodity beat gold over this hundred years. Not one.

scenes.voiceover: So here's the hundred-year scoreboard. Every commodity lost to gold. Stocks are split — Japan's Nikkei is up nine hundred and twenty-two percent, but that number hides a crash from ninety-seven down to twelve. The S&P doubled. The Dow barely doubled. The DAX actually lost money. And gold quietly beat almost everything. The Dow-to-Gold ratio is cyclical — it swings between one and forty-five over decades. Right now, we're at about fourteen. Somewhere in the middle.
